WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The United States needs a new law requiring that the president consult with Congress before going to war, a blue-ribbon panel led by two former secretaries of state said Tuesday. James Baker, left, and Warren Christopher led a panel that recommended a new War Powers Act. The current War Powers Resolution is "ineffective, and it should be repealed and it should be replaced," James Baker said in a joint appearance with Warren Christopher, announcing the results of the study they led. The recommendation follows failed efforts by Democrats in Congress to put a stop to the war in Iraq or to put conditions on President Bush's conduct of it. Congress passed a joint resolution to authorize armed force against Iraq in 2002, but some Bush opponents say it should not have been interpreted as a blank check for the United States to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf nation. Baker, who served in George H.W. Bush's administration, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, said their project was not prompted by any specific war, with Christopher adding that the commission had "tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here." "We didn't direct this report at any particular conflict," Baker added. The existing law, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, has been regarded as unconstitutional by every president since it was passed as a response to the Vietnam War, Baker and Christopher said. It requires presidents to report regularly to Congress about ongoing conflicts, but the provision has been flouted. "No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973," former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the committee, said Tuesday. The panel, formally called the National War Powers Commission, said a new law should be created requiring the president to consult with key members of Congress before sending troops into combat expected to last more than a week, or within three days of doing so in the case of operations that need to be kept secret. It should also make clear exactly who the president needed to consult. The panel suggests that the president talk to "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." The new committee would have a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information, Baker and Christopher said. Congress, in turn, would have to declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within 30 days, they said. If a resolution of approval failed, any member of Congress could introduce a "resolution of disapproval," but it was not clear that such an act would stop a war in progress. Christopher was unable to say in the news conference what practical effect congressional disapproval would have. Baker said the commission had been in touch with the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as leaders of Congress. He declined to reveal what they thought of the proposal, but said: "We haven't gotten a negative reaction." Congress has not officially declared war since 1942, when the United States entered formal hostilities with the Axis powers in World War II. But since then, presidents have sent troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq. The Constitution makes the president the commander in chief of the armed forces, but gives Congress the power to declare war and approve military budgets. Baker and Christopher's group included both Republicans and Democrats and held seven meetings over 14 months.

Announcing the findings of the study they headed, Baker stated during a joint appearance with Christopher that the current War Powers Resolution is "ineffective, and it should be repealed and it should be replaced."

The recommendation follows unsuccessful efforts by Congressional Democrats to halt the war in Iraq or impose conditions on President George W. Bush’s conduct of the conflict. Congress passed a joint resolution authorizing military force against Iraq in 2002, but critics contend it was never intended to serve as an open-ended mandate to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf nation.

Baker, who served under President George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that their study was not prompted by any single war. Christopher noted that the commission "tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here," while Baker added, "We didn't direct this report at any particular conflict."

According to Baker and Christopher, every chief executive since the passage of the 1973 War Powers Resolution—enacted in response to the Vietnam War—has viewed the statute as unconstitutional. Although the existing law mandates that presidents report regularly to Congress regarding active hostilities, this requirement has been routinely disregarded. "No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973," noted former Republican Senator Slade Gorton, a member of the panel.

The group, formally designated as the National War Powers Commission, recommends drafting a new statute requiring the president to consult key lawmakers before deploying troops into combat anticipated to exceed seven days—or within three days of deployment in the case of covert operations.

The proposed legislation would also explicitly define the consultative body. The panel suggests that the president confer with "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." Baker and Christopher explained that this joint committee would be supported by a permanent professional staff equipped with intelligence access.

Under the proposal, Congress would be required to either formally declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within 30 days. If a resolution of approval fails, any member of Congress could introduce a "resolution of disapproval," though it remains unclear whether such a measure could effectively halt an ongoing war. During the news conference, Christopher acknowledged that he could not specify what practical effect congressional disapproval would carry.

Baker disclosed that the commission had consulted with Congressional leaders as well as the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain. While declining to reveal their specific feedback, Baker noted, "We haven't gotten a negative reaction."

Congress has not formally declared war since 1942, when the United States entered hostilities against the Axis powers in World War II. In the decades since, presidents have unilaterally deployed troops to regions including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada, and Iraq. While the U.S. Constitution designates the president as Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, it explicitly assigns Congress the power to declare war and oversee military expenditures.

The bipartisan commission, comprising both Republicans and Democrats, formulated its recommendations after convening seven meetings over a 14-month period.

**Title:** Rebalancing the Sword and the Purse: The Baker-Christopher Commission and the Reform of War Powers

### Introduction
For decades, the constitutional division of war powers between the executive and legislative branches of the United States government has been a source of profound institutional friction. While Article I of the Constitution grants Congress the exclusive power to declare war, Article II designates the President as Commander-in-Chief. In the wake of the Vietnam War, Congress sought to reassert its authority by enacting the War Powers Resolution of 1973. However, the 1973 law ultimately proved ineffective, routinely bypassed by presidents of both parties and criticized as both constitutionally flawed and operationally impractical. 

To break this decades-long stalemate, a distinguished bipartisan panel—co-led by former Secretaries of State James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher—undertook a comprehensive study to rethink how the nation decides to go to war. Their conclusion was unambiguous: the 1973 resolution had failed, and a new, functional framework was urgently needed to ensure meaningful consultation between the President and Congress before American troops are committed to military conflict.

### The Breakdown of the 1973 Resolution
Passed over President Richard Nixon’s veto, the 1973 War Powers Resolution was intended to prevent presidents from slipping into prolonged, undeclared foreign entanglements. It required the chief executive to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying armed forces into hostile situations and mandated that forces be withdrawn within 60 to 90 days unless Congress explicitly authorized the action.

In practice, however, the resolution satisfied neither branch:
* **Executive Objections:** Every administration since 1973 argued that the resolution’s 60-day automatic withdrawal clock was an unconstitutional infringement on executive authority, potentially forcing a commander-in-chief to abandon military operations abruptly.
* **Legislative Impotence:** Presidents routinely circumvented the law by framing operations as brief "humanitarian interventions," "police actions," or limited strikes (such as in Grenada, Panama, Kosovo, and various counterterrorism operations), presenting Congress with a *fait accompli* rather than seeking prior authorization.

Rather than fostering collaboration, the 1973 law resulted in legal evasions and public arguments over process, diverting focus from the strategic and ethical merits of foreign interventions.

### The Baker-Christopher Commission
Recognizing the danger of a broken war powers framework in an increasingly volatile world, the National War Powers Commission was convened in 2007 under the auspices of the University of Virginia’s Miller Center. Co-chaired by James Baker (a Republican) and Warren Christopher (a Democrat), the panel brought together top-tier foreign policy scholars, legal experts, military leaders, and former members of Congress. 

The commission’s mandate was pragmatic: move beyond entrenched ideological and constitutional debate to draft a workable statutory mechanism that respects both the President's need for operational flexibility and Congress's constitutional responsibility to represent the American public on matters of war and peace.

### Key Proposals: The War Powers Consultation Act
In its landmark 2008 report, the panel recommended the complete repeal of the 1973 War Powers Resolution, replacing it with a new statute entitled the **War Powers Consultation Act**. 

The core elements of the proposed framework included:

1. **Mandated Prior Consultation:** The President would be required to consult with Congress prior to ordering military forces into "significant armed conflict"—defined as combat operations expected to last more than seven days. Limited emergency actions, self-defense responses, and covert operations were exempted from prior notice but required immediate post-deployment consultation.
2. **Creation of a Joint Congressional Committee:** To address concerns over security leaks and unwieldy legislative processes, the Act proposed establishing a permanent, bipartisan, bicameral Joint Congressional Consultation Committee. Consisting of House and Senate leadership, along with the chairs and ranking members of the Foreign Relations, Armed Services, and Intelligence committees, this small, high-level body would serve as the President’s primary point of contact for sensitive operational briefings.
3. **Structured Timelines for Congressional Action:** Unlike the 1973 law's automatic withdrawal mandate, the proposed Act required the Joint Committee to introduce a concurrent resolution of approval within 30 days of a deployment. This forced both houses of Congress to record a vote approving or disapproving the conflict, restoring legislative accountability without creating a constitutional standoff over automatic force pullouts.

### Conclusion and Significance
The Baker-Christopher Commission offered a practical, realistic compromise to one of the American republic's oldest legal dilemmas. By shifting the focus from post-hoc legislative vetoes to structured, pre-deployment consultation, the panel created a constitutional model that balances executive decisiveness with democratic accountability. 

While political resistance has left war powers reform unfinished in Congress, the Baker-Christopher framework remains the gold standard for war-powers modernization—a blueprint designed to ensure that when the United States goes to war, it does so with the deliberate, joint consensus of both the President and the representatives of the American public.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — In a rare display of high-stakes bipartisanship, two former Secretaries of State unveiled a sweeping proposal Wednesday to overhaul how the United States decides to go to war, calling for the repeal of the controversial, Vietnam-era War Powers Resolution of 1973.

The proposal, authored by the National War Powers Commission and co-chaired by Republican James A. Baker III and Democrat Warren Christopher, seeks to replace the decades-old law with a new framework designed to force cooperation between the White House and Capitol Hill before American troops are sent into harm’s way.

“The 1973 War Powers Resolution has not worked as intended,” Baker, who served as Secretary of State under President George H.W. Bush, told reporters at the National Press Club. “Every president since its inception has viewed it as unconstitutional, and Congress has repeatedly failed to enforce it. The result has been decades of constitutional brinkmanship and a system that is fundamentally broken.”

The commission's report, sponsored by the University of Virginia’s Miller Center, concludes that the 1973 law—passed in the shadow of the Vietnam War over President Richard Nixon’s veto—has created a dynamic of perpetual political warfare between the executive and legislative branches without effectively restraining presidential authority.

### A New Framework for Conflict

Under the commission's proposed **War Powers Consultation Act**, the 1973 resolution would be officially scrapped and replaced with a structured protocol for military engagement. 

Key elements of the proposal include:

*   **Mandatory Consultation:** The President would be required by law to consult with Congress before ordering U.S. armed forces into "significant armed conflict"—defined as combat lasting or expected to last more than seven days.
*   **A Permanent "War Committee":** To streamline confidential discussions, the law would establish a permanent, bipartisan "Joint Congressional Consultation Committee" consisting of the leadership of both the House and Senate, as well as the chairs and ranking members of the foreign relations, armed services, and intelligence committees.
*   **Forced Congressional Vote:** If the President deploys forces into major combat without prior congressional approval, the new law would require both houses of Congress to vote on a joint resolution of approval or disapproval within 30 days.

Warren Christopher, who served as Secretary of State under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that the goal is not to tie the commander-in-chief's hands in an emergency, but to ensure that the American public, through their elected representatives, has a voice in major conflicts.

“The Constitution envisions a shared responsibility when it comes to the grave decision of sending young Americans into battle,” Christopher said. “Our proposal respects the President’s authority as Commander-in-Chief while restoring Congress to its rightful, constitutional role.”

### Decades of Defiance

The 1973 War Powers Resolution required the executive branch to notify Congress within 48 hours of committing armed forces to military action and forbade armed forces from remaining in state for more than 60 days unless Congress declared war or authorized the use of force.

However, virtually every commander-in-chief since Nixon has questioned the law's constitutionality, arguing it infringes on executive power. From military operations in Grenada and Panama to airstrikes in Kosovo and the broader post-9/11 operations, presidents have consistently notified Congress "consistent with"—rather than "pursuant to"—the 1973 law, sidestepping its actual authority.

Meanwhile, legal experts say Congress has often preferred the political safety of complaining from the sidelines over taking tough, binding votes on military action.

"We have lived under a fiction for 35 years," said CNN Senior Legal Analyst Jeffrey Toobin. "Presidents ignore the law, Congress fumes, and the Supreme Court refuses to get involved. Baker and Christopher are trying to replace a broken legal mandate with a realistic political process."

### An Uphill Battle on Capitol Hill

While the commission boasts a star-studded list of bipartisan foreign policy heavyweights—including former lawmakers, judges, and military leaders—passing the proposal into law will be a formidable task.

Presidents are historically loath to sign legislation that places formal constraints on their military authority, and lawmakers are often hesitant to take on the explicit responsibility of approving dangerous military missions.

Baker acknowledged the political hurdles ahead but urged leaders in both parties to look past short-term political calculations.

"We know this won't be easy," Baker said. "But the current system benefits no one—least of all the men and women in uniform who are put in harm's way without a clear, unified national consensus behind them."

The commission’s draft legislation is expected to be formally introduced in both the House and Senate later this session. White House officials said they were reviewing the report but declined to comment on whether the President would support the measure.

**Bipartisan Panel Led by Baker and Christopher Urges Overhaul of 1973 War Powers Law**

**WASHINGTON** — In a major bipartisan push to resolve a decades-long constitutional deadlock, former Secretaries of State James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher on Tuesday proposed repealing the 1973 War Powers Resolution and replacing it with a new law designed to force the president and Congress to consult before sending U.S. troops into major foreign conflicts.

The proposal, titled the "War Powers Consultation Act of 2009," is the culmination of a 14-month study by the National War Powers Commission, sponsored by the Miller Center of Public Affairs at the University of Virginia. 

The commission’s central recommendation is to do away with the Vietnam-era War Powers Resolution, which every president since Richard Nixon has viewed as an unconstitutional infringement on executive authority, and which Congress has repeatedly proved unable or unwilling to enforce.

Under the proposed statute, the president would be required to consult with a newly established, permanent Joint Congressional Consultation Committee before ordering U.S. armed forces into "significant armed conflict"—defined as combat operations lasting or expected to last more than seven days.

In return, the bill eliminates the most contentious provision of the 1973 law: a mechanism that automatically requires the withdrawal of U.S. troops after 60 days if Congress does not explicitly authorize the deployment. Instead, the new proposal would require both houses of Congress to vote on a joint resolution of approval or disapproval within 30 days of a deployment.

"The 1973 War Powers Resolution has not worked," said Baker, who served as Secretary of State under President George H.W. Bush. "No president of either party has accepted its constitutionality, and Congress has rarely used it effectively. What we need is a practical process that brings the president and Congress together in a spirit of constructive consultation before American lives are put at risk."

Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that the proposal aims to respect the constitutional balances of both branches. "The Constitution grants the president the role of Commander-in-Chief, but it leaves to Congress the sole power to declare war," Christopher said. "Our proposal respects both of those powers, creating a structured, repeatable mechanism that guarantees Congress a seat at the table without hamstringing the chief executive in a crisis."

The proposed Joint Congressional Consultation Committee would consist of 12 key lawmakers, including the majority and minority leaders of the House and Senate, as well as the chairs and ranking members of the Foreign Relations, Armed Services, and Intelligence committees.

The commission’s report comes at a time of heightened debate over executive power, driven by the ongoing conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan and the Bush administration’s broad interpretation of presidential war powers. 

Constitutional scholars and lawmakers largely welcomed the report as a realistic middle ground, though some civil liberties advocates expressed concern that removing the mandatory 60-day withdrawal clock might cede too much authority to the executive branch. Conversely, some executive-power traditionalists questioned whether any statute could mandate presidential consultation without violating Article II of the Constitution.

Baker and Christopher stressed that the timing of the report was deliberate, aiming to present the new administration taking office in January 2009 with a fresh blueprint for foreign policy leadership. 

The co-chairs announced they will formally present the legislation to leadership in both the House and Senate, urging Congress to take up the measure early in the next administration.

**WASHINGTON** — Declaring that the nation’s core mechanism for deciding when to go to war is fundamentally broken, a high-level bipartisan commission led by former Secretaries of State James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher called Tuesday for the complete repeal of the 1973 War Powers Resolution.

Unveiling a proposed replacement law, the National War Powers Commission concluded that the Vietnam-era statute has failed to achieve its goal of balancing war-making authority between the president and Congress. Instead, the panel argued, the 1973 law has been routine ignored by commanders-in-chief of both parties, creating a constitutional stalemate that leaves the nation divided on the eve of military conflicts.

"The 1973 War Powers Resolution does not work," Baker said at a news conference at the National Press Club. "It has neither prevented unconstitutional acts nor promoted timely cooperation between the executive and legislative branches. It is time to replace it with a statute that works."

Christopher echoed his co-chair, noting that the law’s foundational flaws have led every administration since Richard Nixon to view it as an unconstitutional infringement on executive authority.

"The statute has been ignored far more often than it has been honored," Christopher said. "Presidents have taken the position that the law is unconstitutional, while Congress lacks the practical tools to enforce it short of cutting off funding for troops in the field—a step few lawmakers are ever willing to take."

### Why the 1973 Law Failed

The original War Powers Resolution was passed by Congress in 1973 over President Nixon’s veto, driven by public and legislative outrage over the secret bombing of Cambodia and the broader expansion of the Vietnam War. It was designed to rein in presidential power by requiring the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying U.S. armed forces into military action. 

Crucially, the 1973 law mandated that troops must be withdrawn within 60 to 90 days unless Congress explicitly authorized the deployment or declared war.

However, the commission—convened by the Miller Center of Public Affairs at the University of Virginia—found that this automatic "60-day clock" created an unworkable dynamic. Presidents routinely submitted notifications to Congress "consistent with"—rather than "pursuant to"—the resolution, refusing to acknowledge that the statutory clock had begun ticking. 

Opponents in the executive branch argued that Congress could not constitutionally dictate a deadline for military operations through legislative silence. Meanwhile, Congress proved reluctant to invoke the law during ongoing combat operations, fearing that doing so would undermine American troops or signals weakness to adversaries.

### Historical Context: The Vanishing Declaration of War

The commission's report highlighted a glaring historical reality: Congress has not formally declared war since World War II, when it voted to enter the global conflict following the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941.

Despite the United States fighting major, costly conflicts in Korea, Vietnam, the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan, and Iraq, American presidents have relied on alternative authorizations. These include generic authorizations for use of military force (AUMFs), broad United Nations resolutions, or claims of inherent executive authority under Article II of the Constitution as Commander-in-Chief.

While the Constitution grants Congress the sole power to "declare war" in Article I, Section 8, modern warfare moves at a pace that renders formal declarations largely obsolete. The panel argued that this shift has allowed Congress to abdicate its constitutional responsibilities, allowing the president to initiate foreign military commitments unilaterally while lawmakers avoid taking politically risky votes.

### The Proposed Replacement: The War Powers Consultation Act

To resolve this decades-long constitutional deadlock, the Baker-Christopher commission drafted a replacement bill titled the **War Powers Consultation Act of 2008**. 

The proposed legislation discards the controversial 60-day automatic withdrawal clause in favor of a structured, mandatory process designed to force consultation and accountability:

1. **A Permanent Joint Congressional Committee:** The law would establish a standing 12-member congressional committee—comprising the leadership of both parties from the House and Senate, alongside the chairs and ranking members of the Foreign Relations, Armed Services, and Intelligence committees.
2. **Mandatory Prior Consultation:** The president would be legally required to consult with this joint committee *before* ordering U.S. troops into "significant armed conflict"—defined as combat operations that are expected to last more than 30 days or involve direct combat operations. 
3. **A Guaranteed Vote:** If the president initiates significant combat operations, Congress would be required to vote on a joint resolution of approval within 30 days.
4. **No Automatic Cutoffs:** If Congress votes down the resolution, or fails to pass it, the proposed law does not automatically force a troop withdrawal. Instead, it forces Congress to explicitly use its constitutional powers—such as defunding the conflict or passing a joint resolution of disapproval—to halt the war, putting the onus directly on lawmakers.

"What we are proposing is a process that respects the constitutional prerogatives of both branches," Christopher explained. "It brings the president and congressional leadership into the same room before the first shot is fired, ensuring that the nation moves forward with a unified purpose."

### An Uphill Battle in Capitol Hill

The commission presented its findings to President George W. Bush and congressional leaders on Capitol Hill on Tuesday. While the panel boasted a star-studded bipartisan membership—including former Rep. Lee Hamilton, former CIA Director Robert Gates, and former attorney general Edwin Meese—analysts predict that reforming war powers will face significant legislative hurdles.

Presidents may still resist any law that imposes mandatory consultation requirements, viewing it as a potential check on executive power during national emergencies. Conversely, some lawmakers may object to repealing the 1973 law's 60-day mandate, viewing its removal as a concession to the executive branch.

Nevertheless, Baker argued that national security demands a clear, reliable rulebook.

"No law can guarantee wisdom in foreign policy," Baker told reporters. "But a process that fosters genuine, deliberate consultation between the president and Congress will make wise decisions far more likely, and give our men and women in uniform the political support they deserve when they are sent into harm's way."

counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON** — In a bid to end a decades-long constitutional tug-of-war between the White House and Capitol Hill, a high-level bipartisan panel on Tuesday proposed a sweeping overhaul of how the United States goes to war, urging Congress to repeal the 1973 War Powers Resolution and replace it with a system that forces lawmakers to vote on major military actions within 30 days.

The National War Powers Commission, co-chaired by former Secretaries of State James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher, released its long-awaited report following more than a year of study. The panel concluded that the current 1973 law—passed in the shadow of the Vietnam War—is fundamentally flawed, routinely ignored by presidents of both parties, and largely ineffective at ensuring joint decision-making on foreign military interventions.

To bridge the divide between executive speed and legislative oversight, the commission proposed the "Consultation of Powers Act." The centerpiece of the proposal is a mandatory 30-day voting mechanism that would force Congress off the sidelines during national security crises.

### The 30-Day Mechanism

Under the commission’s proposed statute, the president would be required to consult with a newly formed, permanent joint congressional committee before ordering U.S. forces into "significant armed conflict"—defined as combat lasting or expected to last more than seven days.

If the president deploys troops under emergency circumstances without prior consultation, the act triggers a strict legislative clock. Within 30 days of the commencement of hostilities, both the House of Representatives and the Senate would be required to vote on a joint resolution of approval. 

Unlike current law, which theoretically forces a withdrawal of troops after 60 days if Congress does not explicitly authorize the mission—a mandate presidents have argued is an unconstitutional infringement on their duties as Commander-in-Chief—the proposed 30-day mechanism forces an affirmative vote. If Congress votes down the resolution, any member could introduce a joint resolution to force a troop withdrawal or cut off funding, setting up an immediate legislative showdown.

"The goal is not to tie the President's hands, nor is it to let Congress off the hook," Baker said during a news conference at the National Press Club. "It is to ensure that when American men and women are sent into harm's way, the President and Congress stand together."

### Obama and McCain React on the Campaign Trail

The report arrived at a critical juncture in the 2008 presidential race, where the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress has become a central issue following years of controversy over the Bush administration's expansion of presidential authority and the ongoing war in Iraq.

Both major presidential candidates offered measured praise for the commission's bipartisan efforts, though their reactions reflected their differing philosophies on executive power.

Democratic nominee Barack Obama, who built his campaign in part on opposing the Iraq War and criticized executive overreach, welcomed the commission's recommendations as a necessary step toward restoring constitutional balance.

"For too long, Congress has abdicated its constitutional responsibility on matters of war and peace, and the executive branch has operated with too little oversight," Obama said in a statement. The Illinois senator praised the proposed 30-day voting mechanism, noting that "the American people deserve a clear, transparent debate from their elected representatives before our nation enters into armed conflict." Obama committed to working with Congress to modernize war powers legislation if elected.

Republican nominee John McCain, a veteran lawmaker and former prisoner of war, expressed support for the commission's intent to foster better communication between the branches, but was notably more protective of presidential prerogatives. 

Speaking to reporters following a campaign event, the Arizona senator commended Baker and Christopher for tackling a "perennial constitutional conflict," but emphasized that no statute should infringe upon the president's primary constitutional duty to defend the nation.

"I welcome greater consultation between the President and Congress—it is vital for building national consensus," McCain said. "However, as Commander-in-Chief, the President must maintain the authority and flexibility to act decisively to protect American security interests without being paralyzed by legislative gridlock." 

While McCain did not explicitly reject the 30-day voting proposal, aides indicated he harbored reservations about statutory deadlines that might limit an executive's tactical flexibility in a fast-moving global crisis.

### An Uncertain Path in Congress

The commission's report was met with cautious optimism by leaders on Capitol Hill, though legal scholars and veteran lawmakers acknowledged that passing the recommended legislation will be an uphill battle. 

Presidents have historically resisted any legislation that purports to limit their power as Commander-in-Chief, while Congress has often preferred political flexibility over being forced into high-stakes votes on controversial conflicts.

With the November election fast approaching, congressional leaders indicated that formal hearings on the Consultation of Powers Act will likely be deferred until the next administration takes office in 2009. Whoever wins the White House will inherit not only two ongoing wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, but a renewed national debate over who holds the ultimate key to sending Americans to war.

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* Bipartisan panel led by James Baker and Warren Christopher calls for replacing the 1973 War Powers Resolution.
* Proposed "War Powers Consultation Act" would require presidents to consult Congress before major military actions.
* Congress would be forced to vote on military engagements lasting more than 30 days.
* Panel argues the current law is "ineffective and unconstitutional."

---

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — A high-profile, bipartisan panel of statesmen is calling on Congress and the White House to overhaul the way the United States goes to war, arguing that the 1973 War Powers Resolution is deeply flawed and routinely ignored.

The national commission, co-chaired by former Republican Secretary of State James A. Baker III and former Democratic Secretary of State Warren Christopher, released a report Tuesday proposing a new law that would mandate consultation between the president and Congress before American troops are committed to major foreign conflicts.

The proposed legislation, titled the "War Powers Consultation Act," would repeal the 1973 law—passed in the wake of the Vietnam War over President Richard Nixon’s veto—and replace it with a structured framework designed to prevent constitutional standoffs.

"The 1973 War Powers Resolution does not work," Baker said during a news conference presenting the panel's findings. "It has been ignored by every president since its passage, and Congress has rarely tried to enforce it. We need a system that encourages cooperation rather than confrontation."

### A New Framework for Going to War

Under the panel's recommendation, the existing law would be replaced by a streamlined process. Key provisions of the proposal include:

* **A Permanent Joint Committee:** Congress would create a permanent, bipartisan joint committee consisting of key leadership from both the House and Senate, as well as the chairs and ranking members of the foreign relations, armed services, and intelligence committees.
* **Mandatory Consultation:** The president would be required to consult with this joint committee before ordering U.S. armed forces into "significant armed conflict"—defined as combat operations lasting or expected to last more than 30 days.
* **A Forced Vote:** Once consultation occurs, Congress would be required to vote on a joint resolution of approval or disapproval within 30 days of the conflict's commencement.

Unlike the 1973 resolution, which called for an automatic withdrawal of troops after 60 days if Congress did not explicitly authorize the deployment, the new proposal avoids automatic cutoffs. Panel members argued that the automatic withdrawal provision in the 1973 law was likely unconstitutional and created dangerous uncertainty for troops in the field.

### Ending a Decades-Long Struggle

The balance of war powers has been a point of bitter contention between Capitol Hill and the executive branch for decades. While the U.S. Constitution grants Congress the sole power to "declare war," it designates the president as the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

In practice, post-World War II military engagements—from Korea and Vietnam to Iraq and Afghanistan—have rarely involved formal declarations of war, relying instead on broad congressional authorizations or executive action.

Christopher argued that the panel's recommendations would restore the balance intended by the Founding Fathers while accommodating modern military realities.

"No president should go to war without the support of the American people, expressed through their elected representatives in Congress," Christopher said. "This proposal ensures that Congress has a seat at the table before decisions are finalized, not after."

The panel, organized by the University of Virginia's Miller Center of Public Affairs, spent over a year studying the issue, drawing on input from former presidents, military commanders, and constitutional scholars.

It remains uncertain whether Congress or the White House will act on the commission's recommendations, as presidents are traditionally reluctant to cede executive power, and lawmakers are often hesitant to take binding votes on controversial military actions. However, commission members expressed optimism that the bipartisan nature of the proposal could serve as a blueprint for the next administration.
